# Day 3 — Overview {#sec-day3}

Day 1 fitted a model and Day 2 cleaned the data it was fitted to. Both treated
the fitting itself as a single function call: `fit()` in, coefficients out.
Today we open that call. By the end of the day you will have found the same two
numbers four times — by `lm()`, by searching a grid of candidates, by walking
downhill on the loss surface, and by algebra — and you will be able to say which
of those a computer actually does and why.

The thread running through the day is one deliberately unpromising clinical
question:

> **Does a patient's age tell you anything about their blood glucose?**

The answer, on these data, is: almost nothing. That is the point. An exercise
where the model works teaches you the mechanics; an exercise where the mechanics
are perfect and the model is still useless teaches you the difference between
the two.

::: {.callout-note}
## Everything today is in-sample
We fit on all 80 rows and score on the same 80 rows, with no split anywhere.
After @sec-pipeline that should feel wrong, and it is — none of today's numbers
is evidence that anything generalises. Today's question is what fitting *does*,
not how well the result predicts. Held-out evaluation returns on Day 5.
:::

## Objectives

By the end of the day you should be able to, without looking anything up:

::: {.objective-list}
- Distinguish the learning algorithm, the fitted parameters and the dataset, and
  say which of the three a prediction depends on.
- Compute SSR, MSE, RMSE and MAE from a set of residuals, and say what squaring
  does to a badly mispredicted patient that taking the absolute value does not.
- Show that the best fit line depends on the loss you chose, by fitting the same
  data under two losses and getting two different lines.
- Write the gradient descent update rule from memory, and diagnose from a loss
  curve whether the learning rate is too large, too small, or about right.
- Derive the ordinary least squares estimators for one predictor and verify them
  against `lm()`.
:::

## Shape of the day

| | Exercise | Time | Mode |
|---|---------|------|------|
| 3.1 | [Supervised learning](day3-01-supervised-learning.qmd) | 45 min | individual |
| 3.2 | [Loss functions](day3-02-loss-functions.qmd) | 50 min | individual |
| — | break | 15 min | |
| 3.3 | [Gradient descent](day3-03-gradient-descent.qmd) | 60 min | individual |
| 3.4 | [OLS derivation](day3-04-ols.qmd) | 40 min | individual, then pairs |
| — | [Consolidation](day3-99-consolidation.qmd) | 20 min | plenary |

: {tbl-colwidths="[6,52,18,24]"}

Do them in order; the argument is cumulative. 3.2 defines what 3.1 left
undefined, 3.3 solves what 3.2 could only search, and 3.4 shows that for this
one model none of 3.3 was needed.

## What you need before you start

- R and Python working locally, and this project open in your editor
  (@sec-setup).
- `data/diabetes.csv`, which is the module's case study and a synthetic
  replacement for a withdrawn dataset (@sec-data-diabetes). Today we use the
  first 80 rows with a non-zero glucose.
- From Module 2: what a derivative is. You will differentiate $x^2$, a cubic and
  a function of two variables. Nothing harder appears, and @sec-glossary defines
  every term the day introduces.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Running the day.** The emotional arc matters more than usual today. 3.1 ends
with a model that barely beats predicting the mean, 3.2 ends with the best fit
line depending on an arbitrary choice, 3.3 ends with an optimiser that silently
returns nonsense, and 3.4 ends with exact algebra that cannot rescue any of it.
Students who expect a day of reassuring mathematics will need telling, early and
explicitly, that the mathematics is sound and the model is weak, and that these
are separate findings.

**Where the time actually goes.** 3.3 is the long one and the learning-rate table
is its core; protect fifteen minutes for it. 3.4's derivation is worth 20 minutes
only if they write it by hand — reading it achieves nothing. If you are short,
drop 3.4's Task 3 and 3.3's Tasks 2 and 3, in that order; do not drop 3.2, which
everything on Days 4 and 5 assumes.

**Plenary.** Put four numbers on the board — `lm()`'s slope, the grid search's,
the converged descent's and the closed form's — and ask which is the right
answer. They are the same answer, reached four ways, and seeing that written out
is what makes the day cohere.
:::
:::
